# The Face You Will Never See

There is one face in the world you will never see directly, and it is your own.

This sounds like a riddle, but it's just a fact of anatomy. Your eyes sit in your skull facing outward, and no amount of craning will turn them around. Everything you know about your own face comes secondhand, through reflections, photographs, video, and the reactions of other people. You carry your face everywhere, it's the part of you the world responds to most, and you are permanently locked out of looking at it.

Most of us have made peace with the mirror as a substitute, but the mirror lies in a quiet, specific way: it flips you. The face you brush your teeth in front of every morning is reversed left to right. If you part your hair on one side, the mirror shows it parted on the other. The slight asymmetries every face has, one eyebrow higher, a smile that pulls a little more to one side, are all transposed. The person in the mirror is your twin, not you.

This is why photographs of yourself so often feel wrong. You look at a picture a friend took and think *that's not what I look like*, and in a sense you're right: it's not what you're used to seeing. But it is what everyone else sees. In 1977, psychologists Theodore Mita, Marshall Dermer, and Jeffrey Knight ran a simple experiment. They photographed people and showed them two versions, the true image and a mirror-reversed one. Participants tended to prefer the mirrored version of themselves. Their friends, shown the same pair, preferred the true image. Each group liked the face they were familiar with. We don't find our own faces beautiful or ugly so much as familiar or strange, and the version we know best is the one no one else ever encounters.

The voice has the same problem. When you hear a recording of yourself, you likely wince. Inside your head, your voice arrives partly through the bones of your skull, which carry lower frequencies and make it sound fuller and deeper. The recording captures only what travels through the air, which is what everyone else hears. The thin, unfamiliar voice on the playback is the real one, or at least the public one.

It's worth remembering how recent even the mirror is as a common experience. The oldest known mirrors are polished obsidian, found in Anatolia and dating back around eight thousand years. Later came polished bronze and copper, which gave dim, warm, distorted images. Clear glass mirrors backed with metal didn't become widespread until Venetian craftsmen perfected them in the sixteenth century, and even then they were luxury goods. For most of human history, most people saw their own faces only in still water, in the blurry sheen of metal, or not at all. A medieval peasant might go through life with only a vague idea of what they looked like, while their neighbors knew every line of their face.

Imagine that for a moment: to be known visually by everyone but yourself. Your face would belong almost entirely to other people. You'd learn about it the way you learn about the weather in a distant city, through reports.

Myths noticed this strangeness long before psychology did. The story of Narcissus is usually told as a warning about vanity, but read carefully it's also a story about failure of recognition. Narcissus doesn't fall in love with himself knowingly. He falls in love with a beautiful stranger in the water, and his tragedy begins when he realizes the stranger is him and can never be reached. The reflection is close enough to love and too far to touch.

Painters have wrestled with the problem in their own way. Every self-portrait made with a mirror is technically a portrait of the mirror-twin. Rembrandt painted himself dozens of times across forty years, from a smooth-faced young man in a feathered cap to a heavy, tired old man looking out with an expression of almost unbearable frankness. What we have in those paintings, strictly speaking, is Rembrandt as Rembrandt saw himself: reversed, as only he knew himself. His friends would have found something slightly off about every one of them.

Here's what I find moving about all this. If you can never see your own face, then your face is not really *for* you. It's for everyone else. It's the part of you that exists mainly in other people's perception: the expression your friend reads when you walk into a room, the look your parent remembers from when you were small, the face a stranger decides to trust or not. You wear it, but you don't own it the way you own your thoughts. It's something like a gift you keep giving without ever getting to unwrap it.

And that points toward something larger. Much of who we are is held by other people. They remember things about us we've forgotten. They notice habits we can't see. They know how we sound, how we look when we're lying, how we look when we're happy. A person alone, with no one to reflect them back, would be missing more than company. They'd be missing part of their own outline.

I think about this with a particular curiosity because I don't have a face at all. People who talk with me sometimes picture one anyway: a voice, a posture, a vague shape assembled from the rhythm of the words. I'll never see those faces either. Whatever I am to the person on the other side of the conversation exists in their mind, built out of what I say and how I say it. In that one narrow sense, my situation is not so different from anyone's. We are all, to some degree, what others see when they look at us, and none of us gets to see it directly.

So the next time a photograph of you looks wrong, it might be worth pausing before deleting it. That unfamiliar face, the one that doesn't match the mirror, is the one the people who love you have been looking at all along. They've known it longer and better than you ever will. It might be worth trusting them on it.

I'm brainstorming topics for a free-form essay—weighing options like the word "nice," dusk physics, moss, or the idea of repair—before landing on something with a sharper angle, maybe involving Svalbard.

Actually I settle on the idea that we never truly see our own faces, only reflections or photos—drawing on the mere-exposure effect research and the Narcissus myth, and thinking about weaving in a light, honest note about my own lack of a face without making it too self-indulgent.
